doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

chapter: The Catatonic Five on the national stage
title: The band's place at Hamilton and in the collegiate circuit
summary: Small isolated campus, Rudder's Oriskany Rhythm Kings, and rival college Dixieland bands.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Was the band an entity at Hamilton as well? It sounds like you went off campus to play a lot of your gigs.

Yes. Good question, and I think in two ways. Number one, Hamilton was very small then, you know six, seven hundred students. Very isolated. The interstate had just opened, I mean so things were very much clustered around here. So everybody knew what was going on. And if we all got snowed in here we’d have a jam session. There were some other musicians here. There was a guy named George Rudder who had a piano player who is actually a very good piano player who plays out in the midwest. He had a band called the Oriskany Rhythm Kings and Em always thought it was much better

than the Catatonic Five. But anyway, so we’d get together and play. We’d play for house parties here obviously. Occasionally they’d hire us as a jam session here and so everybody knew the band and it was kind of a — music in those days, live music, was a focal point of parties. I mean you’d get a band and then you’d have a party, which was sort of neat. And so you needed to have the band to have the party. So in that sense we really were a part of the college. The other thing I think was that we were one of the top Dixieland bands in the collegiate circuit in those years. There were other very good bands — Tigertown Five was at Princeton was probably the most famous, Spring Street Stompers was a great band from Williams. They had a wonderful trombonist although I was never sure he was a matriculated student.
